Room 1.title: Safe Systems in a Chaotic World
Room 1.track: Functional Programming, AI, Architecture, Ethics, Security
Room 1.abstract:
System failures of all flavors, zero-days, mass layoffs, the climate crisis, AI slop, war, crumbling infrastructure and institutions. Incompetence is so ambient that the term "competency porn" was coined to describe the escapist pleasure of watching someone simply do a thing well.

You cannot control the world, but you can decide what you and your systems will refuse to do. Invariants and the constraints that make them hold are the only way to survive chaos. There is a method for finding them, a discipline for proving they hold, and a runtime built by people who sensed the chaos early.

I'm the CTO of a multinational healthcare software company. I'm in the code with my teams daily. When we think of the term "loss" we're thinking about lives. So we borrow from people who worked the "safety critical" problem before us: systems safety engineering (STAMP and STPA), mistake-proofing from the Toyota Production System, lightweight formal specification, and a virtual machine designed by people who assumed the environments surrounding our code would fail.

You'll leave able to:
- apply safety engineering to shrink the blast radius of LLMs and other threat actors, including ones acting in bad faith
- run continuously available systems on commodity, three-nines cloud junk
- move faster by not breaking things
- find the invariants worth defending, and enforce them where they can't be forgotten under deadline pressure

I've survived thirty-two years in the trenches through several boom-bubble-pop cycles. We're in the most hostile environment I've experienced. These lessons are all I have to offer, and I'm optimistic they will be enough.

Room 1.title: Lambda Calculus - Foundation of Functional Programming
Room 1.track: Functional Programming, JavaScript, Programming Languages, Fun
Room 1.abstract:
You have likely heard the term "Lambda Calculus" several times
throughout your career, but never took the time to learn about it. That was me until recently. Now that I have gone down the rabbit hole, I can assure you that it is a mind-bending experience that is incredibly beautiful!

Lambda Calculus was invented by Elonzo Church in 1936, well before the first computers existed. His goal was to study the nature of functions and how they can interact.

This talk describes the concepts behind Lambda Calculus. It shows how in a system that only provides the ability to refer to variables, define functions, and apply functions, we can perform many operations that we take for granted in programming languages. These include Boolean logic and many forms of arithmetic.

You owe it to yourself to be exposed the amazing capabilities of functions!

Room 1.title: Writing a compiler from scratch
Room 1.abstract:
Have you ever wondered how a compiler works? In this 100% live coding session we'll demystify compilers by building one from scratch!

Our compiler will support a simple, dynamic language with basic math and variables. You'll learn about the different phases of a compiler (lexing/parsing/compiling) and how they build on each other. Finally, we'll bring our language to life by building a runtime that executes our compiled bytecode.

After this session, you'll have a clear understanding how compilers are structured and how to start writing your own!

Room 1.title: Developers in the Dark Forest
Room 1.abstract:
Developers used to have a home on the internet. Stack Overflow was our oracle. Twitter was our town square. Open source repos were our collective workshop. But something has gone wrong. Stack Overflow sits abandoned. Twitter lost its name and its soul. Open source repos are filled with AI-generated code that feels hollow. New "developer platforms" promise community but nobody shows up. The internet isn't just dying for everyone. It's dying for the people who built it.

So we've gone underground into DMs, Discord servers, private Slacks. We're hiding at the edges of a web that doesn't feel like ours anymore. Two theories explain what happened to us. The "dark forest theory" suggests the public internet became hostile: bad actors, bots, trolls, and scrapers turned every public space into a minefield. So we learned to stay quiet, share less, and keep our real conversations private. The "dead internet theory" goes further: most of the content we see online is now generated by bots, for bots. We're not just hiding from threats anymore. We're performing for an audience that might not even be human, contributing to repositories that AI will scrape, answering questions that ChatGPT will repackage. 

This talk explores how these forces changed the developer internet, what it means to build and learn when the web feels broken, and whether we can still find each other.

Room 1.title: Turning microservice chaos into a beautiful concerto
Room 1.abstract:
TL;DR: The demo uses various Dapr workflows, written in C#, to play music with a hardware synthesizer.

Building reliable distributed applications can feel like conducting a sloppy orchestra, where musicians play too loud or can't keep the tempo. As the conductor, you need to set the pace and give instructions to deliver a beautiful performance. When you build microservices and need to coordinate multistep processes, you have to think about the order of execution, time-outs, cascading failures, inconsistent state, and you have very little control to manage the process once it's started.

Dapr Workflow provides a solution through durable execution, a programming model that treats distributed processes like a musical score. Just as a conductor coordinates multiple musicians to play a symphony, Dapr Workflow orchestrates microservices with built-in state persistence, workflow patterns to control the processes in great detail, and workflow management APIs to operate workflows reliably. 

In this session, you'll experience microservice orchestration in a completely new way. I'll run several Dapr workflows, written in .NET, that conduct a musical performance, where each workflow step sends events to a front-end that uses Web MIDI to play virtual and physical instruments in real-time. Watch and hear as distributed services play together! I can't guarantee this performance will be the next Top 40 hit, but it will be fun!

Room 1.title: Locknote: We're Gonna Build an Agent
Room 1.abstract:
"We wanna use one but don't wanna choose one,
Didn't like the others so we'll write another…" ~ Dylan Beattie

"Here we go again." ~ David Guetta.

Right. Fine. Okay then. Let's talk about the great Agentic AI gold rush of 2025–26: the framework explosion, the definitional chaos (is a while loop an agent? discuss), the protocols nobody asked for, and our industry's infuriating habit of solving every new problem by inventing 400 incompatible solutions to it and then arguing on the internet. It is also, in the interests of full disclosure, a talk by someone who is currently building her own agentic coding harness, because of course she is, and who would like to explain, with diagrams, anecdotes and possibly interpretive dance, exactly why that is both completely ridiculous and the only sensible thing to do right now.

Bring your laptop. Don't open it.

Room 2.title: From MVP to GitHub.com: An AI Story of Engineering & Product Collaboration.
Room 2.abstract: Journey through the evolution of GitHub's AI-powered productivity dashboard module from proof-of-concept to a core feature of GitHub's homepage. This session reveals how cross-functional collaboration between engineering, product, and design teams shaped an MVP using Copilot-generated insights into a powerful productivity tool. Learn how the team tackled technical constraints, scaled the solution, and navigated the interplay of engineering and product management. Discover practical strategies for implementing AI features that enhance developer productivity while building trust with users.

Room 2.title: If you thought the speed of writing code was your problem, you have bigger problems
Room 2.abstract:
AI can write code faster than you. Congratulations to the robots. But if speed of code production is the thing holding your team back, I've got some uncomfortable news: you have much bigger problems and nobody is willing to talk about them.

I've spent over 25 years building software and the bottleneck was almost never the typing. It was the three-week argument about what to build. The requirements that changed after you shipped. The stakeholder who couldn't articulate what they actually needed. The architectural decision nobody wanted to own.

Kent Beck said something that stuck with me: 90% of his skills dropped to zero value, but the remaining 10% got a 1000x multiplier. He's right. And the engineers doing well right now (actually well, not performing wellness for LinkedIn) are the ones who figured out which 10% is theirs. They stopped identifying primarily as "people who write code" and started identifying as people who solve problems. Code just happens to be one of the tools.

If your AI strategy is "write code faster," you're optimising the wrong thing.

Let's talk about what to optimise instead.

Room 2.title: Behind the Algorithms: Power, Gender, and Truth in a World Shaped by AI
Room 2.abstract:
For the first time in history, humans speak to computers the way we speak to each other. We ask questions, seek advice, and expect meaningful answers. Large Language Models do more than process commands, they perform conversation and create the illusion of an all-knowing presence.

But who are we really talking to?

Based on ethnographic fieldwork in Silicon Valley and San Francisco, this talk explores the human cultures behind AI. Through interviews and observation among developers, founders, and tech communities, I examine how values, incentives, and worldviews become embedded in systems now used by millions.

LLMs are often presented as neutral tools. Yet they do not simply provide information, they shape what counts as knowledge. Their answers can feel authoritative and true, even when they are partial, biased, or false. This raises urgent ethical questions about truth, accountability, and who gets to define reality through technology.

At a time when “AI ethics” often becomes a vague buzzword, this session offers a sharper map of the terrain: bias matters, but so do power, truth, authority, labor, accountability, and the politics of knowledge production. 

Using gender, especially representations of “the woman,” as a case study, the talk shows how AI systems can reinforce stereotypes while appearing objective.

This session is for developers, leaders, policymakers, and anyone trying to navigate the ethical landscape of AI.

Room 2.title: Bobbysocks commit
Room 2.track: People, DevOps, Soft Skills, Testing, Web, Work Skills
Room 2.abstract:
Why do we dare to push code during the last performance of MGP, 5 minutes before the voting starts?

Time is 20:34, 15th of february 2025, I am sitting in a dark room behind the stage in Oslo Spektrum, cheers sounding from the crowd. On my Mac, I can see hundreds of complaints from users who can't get into our webapp. In 26 minutes, when the voting intro with a QR code to our page runs live on TV, I know there will some hundred thousand new users arriving. What do I do?
My team delivers audience interaction for big live-events in NRK TV. It involves hard deadlines, large spikes in traffic in really short timeframes which are mostly outside our workhours.
What do we do to make sure our systems perform when they need to? What securitymeasures do we have in our deployment pipelines? How do we know that the users actually get our new code?
Lets talk about socio-technical safety.

Room 2.title: Unf*ck your mind: How to finally build something great again
Room 2.abstract:
Let’s be honest: your mind is f*cked. Overloaded, overstimulated and drowning in an endless to-do list. Everything needed to be done yesterday, you’re pulled in a hundred directions, and somewhere along the way, you forgot what actually matters.

We’re bombarded with notifications, meetings, and meaningless busywork. AI is making it worse spitting out endless streams of generic, forgettable content. We move faster and produce more, but are we actually creating anything worth remembering?

The result? Mediocre, half-assed outcomes. Not just in your work, but everywhere in your company, with your customers, in your career. We’re all stuck in this cycle, rushing to meet deadlines we didn’t set, for work that isn’t great, while convincing ourselves that speed equals value.

This session is about breaking that cycle. It’s about unf*cking your mind so you can focus on what actually matters and finally build something you’re proud of.

After this session, you will:

-> Know how to unf*ck your brain and work like a person, not a machine.
-> Know how to spot the fake urgency that’s keeping you from real progress
-> Build the best product or service you’ve ever created
-> Tell the difference between what’s actually important and what only seems important

Room 3.title: Does This PR Lower the Energy State?
Room 3.abstract:
What if software architecture isn't just best practices, but follows the laws of physics? This talk introduces the Energy State Principle, a new way of thinking that applies thermodynamic laws to software development decisions.

Just as physical systems naturally evolve toward low-energy states, software systems have natural configurations that minimize cognitive energy. We'll explore how entropy accumulation explains why codebases decay into "big balls of mud," why static typing reduces system energy, and why premature abstraction violates the laws of nature.

Through concrete examples - from Python's Any type (maximum entropy) to perfect domain boundaries (minimum energy states), you'll learn to evaluate architectural decision by asking: "Does this bring the system to a lower energy state?"

Walk away with a new way of thinking about code reviews, refactoring decisions, and architectural planning that works with natural forces instead of fighting them.

Room 3.title: Functional Programming with the aid of AI
Room 3.abstract: Functional programming is a great alternative to imperative style of programming due to reduced complexity and ease of maintenance. However, most programmers have spent more time learning and practicing imperative style and often find it hard to program in the functional style. Hey, why not use AI to create functional style code? Great thought but we can't simply put AI on autopilot on this one. In this presentation, we will take an example driven approach to understand the power and perils of using AI to create functional style code.

Room 3.title: Code Once, Pin Everywhere: Multiplatform Widgets for Android & iOS
Room 3.abstract:
Widgets are back in style — and now, they live on both Android and iOS home screens.
But maintaining two separate implementations, two data flows, and two update mechanisms? That’s a headache.
In this session, we’ll explore how Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) can unify your widget logic across platforms, letting you share state, data, and update code while keeping native UIs through Glance (Android) and WidgetKit (iOS).
You’ll learn how to architect a shared KMP core that powers both widgets and apps, manage reactive updates via Flows, and handle background refresh with minimal duplication.
A live demo will show a single shared Kotlin module driving widgets on Android and iOS — proving that even the smallest UI can benefit from shared logic.

Room 3.title: Demand-Driven Context: What 300 Incidents Reveal About Tribal Knowledge
Room 3.abstract:
RAG can't retrieve what was never documented. Fine-tuning can't learn what only exists as institutional habit. And yet that's exactly where enterprise knowledge lives — in chat threads, runbooks nobody reads, and the heads of experienced staff.

We gave an AI agent 300 real production incidents from a retail e-commerce platform and asked it to resolve them. It failed — repeatedly, predictably, and in ways that told us exactly what knowledge was missing. It didn't know that the nightly batch job retries three times before escalating to the on-call team. That "fulfilment window expired" means something different in the Nordic region than in Central Europe. That the inventory service was migrated eighteen months ago but three teams still call it by the old name.

We developed Demand-Driven Context (DDC), a methodology inspired by Test-Driven Development: instead of documenting everything upfront and hoping it's useful, we let the agent fail on real problems, identify exactly what knowledge is missing, and curate only the minimum context needed to succeed. Failure is the signal for what to document.

After nine DDC cycles, the agent produced a reusable knowledge base of 46 entities — and we observed convergence: each new incident required fewer new entities because previous cycles had already captured overlapping knowledge.

This talk walks through the methodology, the convergence data, and a scaling architecture for running DDC across domains.

Room 3.title: Pwned with Purpose: Where Motives Meet Mayhem
Room 3.abstract: Every data breach tells a story — not just of compromised information, but of human motive. Drawing on a dozen years of experience running Have I Been Pwned, this talk explores why hackers exfiltrate and share data, what those motives reveal about the evolving threat landscape, and how understanding them helps us respond more effectively in partnership with website operators.

Room 4.title: Demoscene Coding Kickstart
Room 4.abstract:
Ever heard of the demoscene? It is this amazing community of recreational and competitive programmers. The point is to use code to create the most amazing graphical creations and impress everyone with artistic algorithmic brilliance.

The demoscene taught me so much about being a good programmer, and I thought I'd give you all the opportunity to join in on the fun and learn how to create some great demos! 

I will guide you through the following:
- Old school demo effect concepts
- Modern-day demo effect concepts
- Entry to shadercoding on Directx12
- Tools of the trade
- How to be creative with mathematics
- Bringing it all together to a demo-concept

So bring out your graphic calculators, and let's get those techno beats going and learn how to paint and create worlds with maths!

Room 4.title: Copy & Paste the World with Gaussian Splatting
Room 4.abstract:
Recent advances in Gaussian Splatting have made the generation of 3D scenes from video and photos faster, better, and more accessible. You can now use your smartphone, or a drone, or any other camera to generate a realistic 3D scene that can be rendered in the web browser, or immersively in VR.  

In this talk I will show how these 3D scenes can be generated, edited and displayed. At the end of the talk you will be able to generate your own Gaussian Splats of the real world, and know how they can be shared with others.

Room 4.title: The Undersea Infrastructure
Room 4.abstract: Beneath the world’s oceans lies a vast and largely unseen network of critical infrastructure that powers modern civilization. Join Richard Campbell as he explores these undersea connections, how they are built, maintained, repaired, and continue to evolve. Modern events show that this infrastructure can be part of warfare, which has significant consequences for the world. Together, these intertwined data, electrical, and petrochemical networks form the hidden circulatory system of the planet—vital, complex, and increasingly essential to global stability and progress.

Room 4.title: Build 2.5D and 3D immersive map experiences in a browser
Room 4.abstract:
The world of web-based mapping has evolved far beyond simple pin drops on a flat surface. Modern browsers can now render incredibly rich, immersive geographical visualizations that make users feel like they're flying through real world. Whether it is your morning bike ride, a historical journey record or a log of pizza deliveries, you can put all such data on a web page and animate it smoothly. Join me on the journey into modern mapping technologies to find the best approach for your use case!

We'll explore the full spectrum of possibilities - from traditional 2D maps to photorealistic 3D city skylines. We'll start with the fundamentals of efficient tile-based mapping systems and satellite imagery integration, then progressively add complexity, depth and... fun(!) to our visualizations. On the way, we will check what is this 2.5D all about and how it uses file formats dating back to... fax machines! We will also combine the experience from gaming to add a thrill to the camera movement.

Through live examples and code snippets, you'll learn how to implement these techniques using popular front-end frameworks and mapping libraries. By the end of the session, you'll have practical knowledge of both the implementation details and UX considerations that make these visualizations truly immersive.

Room 4.title: Bootable applications - next steps
Room 4.abstract:
This is a follow up to my previous session "Bootable applications - an introduction". It is not required as we will briefly summarize the key takeaways allowing us to move further.

In this session we will investigate how to build complete interactive programs such as games and UI-driven applications, still without ever booting into your regular operating system. Learn what is possible as we throw away some tens of millions lines of code we have learned to depend and rely on every day!

We will utilize UEFI-complient systems, allowing us to boot it on any compliant PC system / emulator (e.g. qemu). We'll use the system level languages Zig and C for the examples.

Room 5.title: Platform Engineering Beyond the Tools: Lessons Learned Across Industries
Room 5.abstract:
Platform Engineering promises to accelerate development, simplify operations, and enhance productivity across software organizations. But what separates thriving platform teams from those that struggle to deliver on these promises?
In this talk, we’ll explore lessons from real-world experiences across diverse sectors—media, online marketplaces, surveillance, and banking. From successes and failures, we’ll highlight common pitfalls, practical strategies, and the crucial importance of adopting a product-oriented mindset. We’ll delve into why platform engineering must move beyond mere tool adoption to embrace company culture, engineering practices, team capabilities, and internal advocacy.
You’ll walk away with a practical framework to evaluate your own platform engineering maturity. Join this session to understand how your approach measures up and what steps you can take to evolve your platform engineering journey effectively.

Room 5.title: From 2am Alert to Post-Mortem: Building a Multi-Agent SRE System with CAIPE
Room 5.abstract:
It's 2am. PagerDuty fires. You're jumping between Kubernetes dashboards, log aggregators, Slack threads, and runbooks. The context-switching under pressure piles up while the clock runs. This is the environment we designed CAIPE for.

CAIPE (Community AI Platform Engineering) is an open-source multi-agent system built under CNOE (Cloud Native Operational Excellence) that coordinates specialized AI agents across the full platform engineering lifecycle: incident detection, triage, remediation, deployment management, and post-mortem generation. But this isn't a project demo: it's an engineering story about what it actually takes to make multi-agent systems work under operational constraints.

We'll walk through the architectural decisions that actually matter: why a supervisor-agent model outperformed a flat agent mesh for incident workflows, where MCP and A2A protocols solved real coordination problems (and where they didn't), and how this environment has kept on growing with the collaboration of the open-source community - based on personal experiences as a repository mantainer and user for data network operations. You'll see the system handle a live incident scenario end-to-end: not a happy path, but a realistic one with noise, ambiguity, and competing signals.

You'll leave with a clear model for designing multi-agent systems based on CAIPE, as well as guidance on how to collaborate to this open-source project.

All demo repositories will be made available.

Room 5.title: From Noise to Signal: Building Meaningful SLIs in Azure
Room 5.abstract:
Most systems today are over-instrumented and under-observed.
Discover how to build meaningful Service Level Indicators (SLIs) that reflect real user experience—not just system metrics. This session shows how to instrument SLIs with OpenTelemetry, connect them to Azure’s Health Model, and turn raw telemetry into actionable reliability signals that drive SLOs, error budgets, and deployment gates.

Designed for developers who want to own reliability from day one and move beyond noisy dashboards to observability that truly matters.

Room 5.title: Magical client-side logging – the little headers that could
Room 5.abstract:
In a server-side app, it's fairly easy to find out what went wrong from logs. But what about the client side, where you don't have the luxury of consistency or reliable controls in an often hostile environment? The W3C's Reporting API and associated HTTP headers can let you know about all kinds of client-side issues that you'd otherwise never see. Reveal problems related to content security policy, network error logging, CSP hashes (give your SBOMs a workout!), permissions policy, and even browser crashes.

The standards covering these useful features are in a state of flux, and suffer from inconsistent implementation across browsers, so I'll guide you through what works, what doesn't, how to make them all work everywhere, and how to use aggregation services to make sense of all the new data you're getting. 

We'll put it all together, and solve all the issues that only your customers have been seeing!

Room 5.title: Stop scaling and start tuning
Room 5.abstract:
When a database is slow, you have two options: burn more money with your cloud provider, or roll up your sleeves and fix it. Many teams click the scale up button first - more RAM and CPU takes 60 seconds and buys them time. But it inevitably comes back worse than before.

My team recently faced the same situation. Scaling up resources had deferred the problem for awhile, but it was time to figure out what was going on. Our system was overwhelming the database in multiple ways: missing indexes, N+1 queries, ORM malfeasance, even a dodgy connection pool.

This talk will walk you through the process we used to fix them: how to decipher telemetry, review query plans, and tune indexes or data access patterns. The issues we uncovered are common in many database applications and you’ll come away with a practical blueprint for resolving them.

Room 6.title: Aspire Beyond the Introduction
Room 6.abstract:
You have probably already seen a bunch of introductions to Aspire. Maybe to the point where it is getting a bit boring, even if it is cool!

In this talk, we will take it a step further and look into some more advanced topics around Aspire. The things that takes it from a cool demo, to a really helpful tool for you development.

The focus of the talk, is to cover what is really happening when you use it. Knowledge that lets you know how to tweak it to your need, when you needs aren't covered out of the box. 

It will also cover how you can build your own extensions to Aspire, to allow you to use it for your custom applications, or projects that aren't already supported by the community. Things like creating your own Aspire resources and custom commands.

Room 6.title: Building well-documented versioned HTTP APIs in ASP.NET Core
Room 6.track: .NET, Architecture, DevOps, Programming Languages, Testing, Tools
Room 6.abstract:
Anybody that has built HTTP or REST APIs, has had to deal with things like OpenAPI or Swagger. Those are reasonably trivial to implement using ASP.NET Core, and you even get a nice Swagger UI website out of the box. 

Just like any interface or programmatic contract, there are plenty of aspects that need careful analysis. Think of comprehensive online documentation for your APIs, using HTTP error codes appropriately, and providing clarity on what fields in the JSON are required and which are optional or can be empty. And don't forget versioning. Allowing a developer to view and switch between the supported versions and make it clear what APIs are deprecated isn't as trivial as you may think. 

In this talk, I'll show you everything that you might need to know about building nicely documented, properly versioned HTTP APIs that make your consumers happy.

Room 6.title: Secure and Compliant APIs - By Design
Room 6.abstract:
If you ask 10 developers for a code review, they will identify different issues, and many will miss security concerns like broken access control and lack of input validation. 
 
How can a DevOps team in their daily work assert that new features do not introduce vulnerabilities,  that security bugs get caught before deploy to production? What are the key questions to ask in a code review? And how can we show that the application code also aligns with requirements from compliance, well-known best practices and internal security policies?
 
This presentation will demonstrate how to build APIs that are both secure and compliant by design; using OWASP ASVS and support from an application security tuned coding agent. 
 
Demos will be for an API in .NET with Copilot custom agents.

Room 6.title: Who to blame? The AI, The Programmer, or The Prompt?
Room 6.track: Security, AI, Architecture, DevOps, Ethics, Security, GenAI
Room 6.abstract:
This interactive session transforms AI security education into an engaging courtroom style debate. We'll present five critical vulnerabilities affecting modern AI development tools, and after each case study, the audience becomes the jury—voting on who's responsible: the careless user, the negligent developer, or the inadequate service provider.

We'll dissect real CVEs including GitHub Camo Leak (CVE-2025-59145), Ollama RCE (CVE-2024-37032), AWS MCP Server Shell Injection (CVE-2025-5277), Anthropic MCP Inspector DNS Rebinding (CVE-2025-49596 ) and Microsoft Copilot's zero-click data exfiltration (CVE-2025-32711). Each case reveals technical root causes through collaborative analysis.

The conclusion challenges the "blame game" itself: these vulnerabilities expose fundamental architectural weaknesses in agentic AI systems where traditional security models fail. We'll establish that securing AI tools demands a shared responsibility framework developers must code defensively, providers must architect securely, and users must understand AI-specific risks.

Room 7.title: Accessibility and Computer Vision: Building A System for the New York Times
Room 7.track: Accessibility, AI, Big Data, Cloud, Mobile
Room 7.abstract:
This session introduces an accessibility feature built into the New York Times News Reader app. Designed for people with vision impairments, the tool acts as an in-app AI lens that interprets complex visual content—like infographics, data visualizations, and interactive elements—using natural language voice descriptions.

The goal is to improve accessibility across the app’s interactive experiences by providing real-time, AI-powered narration that describes not just what’s on the screen, but what it means. Whether it's a chart explaining election results or an interactive timeline of climate data, the system helps users understand the structure, intent, and insight behind the visuals.

Key topics in this talk:

Designing an accessible layer that integrates with the existing rendering stack in a production news app

Using computer vision to segment and classify app components like graphs, images, and interactives

This prototype was developed during MakerWeek 2024 as part of ongoing accessibility research at The New York Times. It reflects a practical, thoughtful application of AI to improve how people with low vision can experience and understand news content on mobile.

Keywords: accessibility, Android development, computer vision, assistive technology, AI narration, data visualization, on-device inference, voice interface.

Makerweek 2024 Talk: https://youtu.be/5V5Puneu9l4

Room 7.title: How I built my own intelligent Robot Arm from Scratch
Room 7.abstract:
Are you tired of the same old AI, LLM, buzzword sessions and wondering if there is still anything new and cool out there we can do with AI? Do you crave an exciting, slightly ridiculous project that's just a lot of fun - while also learning about a whole new field with lots of promise? Don't miss this session!
Physical AI is about bringing together all the amazing breakthroughs (yes, like large language models) into the fields of robotics and embedded systems. We can make autonomous robots and systems that can generate their own movement instructions and evolve, without having to painstakingly define all the complex code or even tiny physics-engine implementations to get going.
But first - we need to build actual robots! As someone coming from the data science field - this may sound like a bit of a leap.
However, with a "I'm sure it can't be that hard" attitude, a bunch of electronics components, and an uncontainable enthusiasm - I set out to do just that.
I will share the story of building my own Robot Arm from 0 to an incrementally more complex prototype, and how I started giving it some "AI superpowers", and what's next in this exciting field!

Room 7.title: Lightning Talks 5
Room 7.track: Programming Languages, AI, Architecture, People, Tools, Work Skills, GenAI
Room 7.abstract:
Lightning talks (approx 10-15 minutes each)

Talk 1: When the code is not working for you - Helén Persson
Code can be running fine, but still not work great for us as humans. Maybe you have inherited a piece of legacy code? Maybe you are drowning in Dependabot alerts? Lets talk about how you can leave the code base better than when you found it.


Talk 2: Knitting is programming - Njord Solberg
Did you know that knitting can be considered one of the origins of computer science? No? Neither did a group of teachers I once taught block programming. But they were fascinated to learn the story of how knitting has influenced modern computer programing. Hopefully, you will be as fascinated by the story as they were.

Talk 3: AI Moved the Bottleneck. It Didn't Remove It - Anders Erlandsen
In March 2026, I launched Spillmakker — a matchmaking app for people who want to play padel, tennis, or climb but don't know who with. Three weeks later: 293 users, 106 matches, 255 messages. Built solo, evenings only, zero budget. Every line of code was written by an AI agent.
This isn't a talk about how AI will change software. It's a field report from already having done it.
I'll show you the actual architecture — Next.js, Supabase, RLS, production-grade tests — and more importantly, the seven markdown files I use to steer Claude Code autonomously. Not prompts. Role documents. Principles encoded as text.
The surprising finding, coming from seven years of product leadership in regulated industries: when the AI can build anything, the real work moves up the stack. Technical feasibility is no longer the hard part. Judgment is. Prioritization is. Knowing what not to build is.
You'll leave with a concrete method for principle-driven AI development, honest numbers on what works and what doesn't, and one uncomfortable observation about where developer skill is heading.

Talk 4: Pixels to Intelligence: A Computer Vision Pipeline for Overhead Satellite Imagery - Gayathri Palani
Satellite imagery is just pixels until you build the pipeline. Whether you're counting cars in a retail parking lot or monitoring turbine conditions at a wind farm, the underlying engineering challenge is the same: turn raw overhead imagery into a reliable, time-series signal you'd actually trust.
In this lightning talk, I'll walk through the core architecture of a production-grade overhead object detection pipeline — one pattern, two real-world applications. We'll cover the decisions that actually matter: sourcing and preprocessing imagery across satellite resolution tiers (30cm vs 50cm vs 3m and what you lose at each step), model selection for top-down detection tasks (YOLO variants, fine-tuned vision models, and where large vision LLMs genuinely fall short), handling the label scarcity problem specific to overhead imagery datasets, and aggregating detection outputs into time-series signals with meaningful confidence bounds.
We'll be honest about the hard parts — shadow artefacts, temporal cadence constraints, false positives in dense scenes, and the gap between a compelling notebook demo and a system that runs reliably in production.
You'll leave with a concrete pipeline blueprint for overhead CV tasks, a clear model selection framework, and a realistic map of where satellite AI is mature versus where the friction is still real.

Room 7.title: Lightning Talks 6
Room 7.track: Programming Languages, AI, DevOps, Machine Learning, Security, Fun, GenAI
Room 7.abstract:
Lightning talks (approx 10-15 minutes each)

Talk 1: When AI writes the code, what do we do? - Tomas Hensrud Gulla
We live in a time where we can write code without understanding it. AI makes us faster, more productive, and less tired.
But what if programming isn’t just about efficiency?
What if it’s also about resistance?
Maybe the developer of the future doesn’t need to write more code. Maybe we need to play with it more.
I’ll show you examples of code written in some very different languages.
One language probably belongs on a wall. One you can’t even see. One should be performed at full volume. And the last one you absolutely cannot sit still while writing it.
This is part performance, part talk. Part humour, part serious.


Talk 2: How hunting for an attack surface, led me to the front-doors of wind turbines - Knut Erik Hollund
As a relatively new in the field of cybersecurity, with a primary focus on Application Security (AppSec), I have been intrigued by the methods attackers use to identify their attack surfaces. In preparation for an internal presentation at our company, I embarked on a project to explore potential attack surfaces using various tools. My objective was to identify a wind turbine farm located in Europe. This endeavor was aimed at illustrating the Secure Design principle - "defense in depth."
During my presentation, I will guide the audience through my journey, starting from the initial question to the point where I reached the front door of the wind turbine farm. It involves tools as AI and Shodan.io.

Talk 3: Breaking the Corporate Firewall: How to get a little AI into your very large company - Sean Percival
Your company is falling behind on AI. You know it. Your competitors know it. And somewhere deep in a conference room, a committee is meeting about it — which means nothing is going to happen for another eighteen months.

This talk is not about waiting for permission.

It's about how individuals — not executives, not transformation teams, not consultants — are the ones who actually change how large organizations work. One quiet experiment at a time. One small win that can't be ignored. One person who decided to stop waiting and start doing.

"In Norway, the fastest way to do something big is to start embarrassingly small."

The corporate firewall is real. Legal will say no. IT will say no. Procurement will say nothing for six weeks and then say no. But there is a way through — and it starts with you, a low-stakes test, and a result nobody can argue with.

Why large companies stall on AI — Death by committee. The approval loop. Why "we need a strategy" means nothing is happening.
Start embarrassingly small — One team. One tool. Four weeks. One metric. Why tiny experiments are the only things that actually get approved.
Isolate the blast radius — How to ring-fence risk so legal, IT, and compliance can say yes. The sandbox framing that unlocks everything.
Show results first, ask for permission later — Why data is the only currency that moves Norwegian organizations — and how to document obsessively so the numbers do the lobbying.

Workshop room.title: Part 1/2: Practical Domain-Driven Design - A Modeling Exercise
Workshop room.track: DDD, Architecture, People, Soft Skills, Testing
Workshop room.abstract:
If you are involved in almost any role related to software product development then you are, by definition, doing modeling. There is always a distinction between the real world and a software product, and the difference is in the model by which the software product chooses to describe the reality.

In this workshop you will practice modeling in order to become better at designing, organizing and building software products. 

You will be guided to think from different perspectives and to produce multiple models for the same domain problem. We will cover four different modeling approaches, each bringing more nuance and detail in the understanding of the domain:
* Functional decomposition
* Role-based decomposition
* Time- and role-based decomposition
* Decomposition by business capabilities

The real-world problem from the domain of healthcare will be a foundation for the exercise.

Since product development is a cross-functional approach, this exercise will benefit from cross-functional mixture of participants. You are hereby encouraged to join the workshop, regardless of your role in software product development.

Workshop room.title: Part 1/2: A Practical TDD Journey with AI
Workshop room.abstract:
Designing Quality from the First Test

In this hands-on session, participants will learn how to apply the principles of Test-Driven Development (TDD) while pairing with AI-powered tools to accelerate test creation and improve code quality.
Through guided coding challenges, developers will start from the red-green-refactor loop and explore how AI can assist in writing meaningful tests, suggesting implementations, and reinforcing strong design habits.
The workshop focuses on helping participants gain confidence using AI as a collaborator and enhancing, not replacing, human judgment; to produce well-designed, maintainable code.

By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

- Understand the TDD workflow and apply it to build a small REST API from scratch
- Use AI tools to generate initial test scaffolding and refine test cases through context and feedback
- Practice the red-green-refactor loop to validate both test quality and implementation correctness
- Identify design and testing smells introduced by AI-generated code
- Reflect on responsible and ethical use of AI in software development
